strengths: The framework is genuinely general: it wraps around an arbitrary base inference procedure (conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided testing, outlier detection, multiple testing) under a single theory, and the partial-order formulation (Condition F.1) cleanly captures unions/intersections and OR/AND operations.

The theoretical guarantees are clean, distribution-free, and finite-sample. Theorem 3.2 gives risk ≤ α + min{ε, c·d(P,Q)} regardless of synthetic data quality, and the two-sided version (Theorem 3.3 / F.2) deterministically sandwiches the output between Alg_α and Alg_{α+ε}, which is a strong, easy-to-interpret validity statement.

The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) is insightful: it shows that uniformly controlling the risk at level α for all possible synthetic distributions is unattainable without effectively discarding the synthetic data, which motivates the α+ε relaxation well.

The empirical study is diverse and applied to real, non-trivial settings: AlphaFold2 conformal risk control, LLM win-rate comparison on AIME25, outlier detection with contaminated reference sets, and mechanistic interpretability of a CLIP ViT attention head, with consistent evidence that GESPI controls error near nominal while improving power/reducing abstention.
The paper is clearly written and the 'black-box wrapper' framing is intuitive and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core mechanism—running a synthetic-powered procedure and taking the min (intersection/AND) with a relaxed-level (α+ε) guardrail on real data—is a fairly direct generalization of Synthetic-Powered Predictive Inference (Bashari et al., 2025a). The advance is mainly in generality rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The central bound (Theorem 3.2) depends on the total-variation distance between the loss distributions under (P,Q) and (Q,Q), which is not estimable in practice. As a result the bound functions more as an interpretation than an actionable quantity, and the claim that GESPI 'mimics the effect of applying the base method to a larger real dataset' is heuristic rather than quantified.

The advertised 'adaptivity' to synthetic data quality is largely qualitative: the method does not detect whether synthetic data are good or bad, and realized gains depend on the user-chosen tolerance ε, for which little principled guidance is provided (only sensitivity ablations).

Experimental scale is modest (e.g., n=10 CASP-14 proteins, 30 AIME25 problems, 40–100 clean inliers), and some synthetic-data constructions are contrived—e.g., treating AlphaFold MSAs as synthetic data with PAE-based proxy errors, where true structures are unavailable—which weakens the strength of the empirical claims.
Despite explicitly positioning GESPI as a generalization of SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a), no direct head-to-head empirical comparison with SPI is provided to substantiate the claimed improvements.

strengths: Proposes a general wrapper (GESPI) that can turn any base inference method into one that safely leverages synthetic data, with applicability to conformal prediction, hypothesis testing, outlier detection, multiple testing, and more.
Provides distribution-free, finite-sample risk-control guarantees that hold without assumptions on the synthetic distribution (though at the relaxed level α+ε).
The method is simple and computationally cheap: it only requires three runs of the base algorithm and a min/max aggregation.
Includes a diverse set of experiments spanning protein structure prediction, LLM win-rate testing, outlier detection, and mechanistic interpretability of a vision transformer.
The theoretical framework using partial orders and monotone losses is general and cleanly abstracts several classical inference problems.
weaknesses: The flagship protein-structure experiment violates the independence assumption required by the theory: synthetic data are constructed from MSAs of the same real CASP-14 proteins, so D_n and Dhat_N are not independent draws from P and Q. The claimed distribution-free guarantee therefore does not apply to this experiment, undermining its empirical support.

No comparison to the closest baseline, Synthetic-Powered Predictive Inference (SPI; Bashari et al., 2025a), despite SPI being the direct inspiration and a natural state-of-the-art method for conformal prediction with synthetic data. The experiments only compare to OnlyReal and OnlySynth, which are not sufficient to establish improvement over existing synthetic-powered methods.

The methodological novelty is limited: GESPI is essentially a simple wrapper that runs the base method at α+ε and at α on pooled data, then takes min/max. The theoretical results are straightforward consequences of monotonicity and bounded loss, and the advance over SPI is incremental.

The guarantee is at level α+ε, not α. When synthetic data are poor, the method can have higher error than the base method (up to α+ε). The abstract and introduction imply a stronger default-to-standard behavior than is actually guaranteed; the base method's α-level control is not preserved in the worst case.

The key quantity in the bound, d_{ℓ,Alg}(P,Q), is an algorithm- and loss-specific total-variation distance between loss distributions, not a standard or practically estimable measure of synthetic data quality. It is neither estimated nor validated in the experiments, so the theoretical improvement over α+ε remains largely abstract.

The protein experiment uses predicted alignment error (PAE) as a proxy for true per-residue error in the synthetic data, and the synthetic data are derived from the same proteins as the real data. This can leak information and makes the empirical risk control less convincing.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data availability statement is provided, and the protein pipeline depends on specific AlphaFold/ColabFold databases and preprocessing choices that would be difficult to reproduce exactly.

Some experimental details are unclear (e.g., independence between clean and contaminated reference sets in outlier detection, exact test-set splits in LLM experiments), and several plots lack uncertainty quantification such as confidence intervals or error bars.
The limitations discussion is incomplete: it does not acknowledge the independence-assumption violation in the protein experiment, the α+ε tradeoff, or the lack of comparison to SPI.

strengths: The GESPI framework is genuinely general and elegant: by treating the base inference procedure as a black box and aggregating three runs (base at α, guardrail at α+ε, synthetic-powered at α) via min/max operations, it applies uniformly to conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, multiple testing, and outlier detection. This is a meaningful conceptual advance over SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a), which modifies the internals of conformal prediction rather than wrapping around arbitrary procedures.

The theoretical results are clean and well-supported. Theorem 3.2 gives a distribution-free upper bound α + min{ε, c·d_{ℓ,Alg}(P,Q)}, and Theorem 3.3/F.2 establish the deterministic sandwich Alg_α(D_n) ⪯ Ãlg(D_n, D̂_N) ⪯ Alg_{α+ε}(D_n), which directly implies that GESPI never loses power relative to the base method while never exceeding the guardrail level. The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) is a nice addition justifying why α+ε (rather than α) is the appropriate worst-case target, and the tailored bounds (Theorem H.1, H.3) add concreteness.

The empirical evaluation is diverse and covers genuinely challenging applications: AlphaFold2 protein structure prediction with conformal risk control, LLM win-rate comparison on AIME25, conformal outlier detection on three tabular benchmarks, and mechanistic interpretability of a CLIP ViT attention head. The protein experiment (Figures 2, 3) is especially compelling—GESPI achieves risk near the nominal level while substantially reducing the abstention rate relative to OnlyReal.

Reproducibility is adequate: the appendix specifies model checkpoints, prompts, hyperparameters, dataset splits, and the answer-verification protocol (math_verify plus an LLM judge), and the experimental procedures are described in sufficient detail to be replicated.

The limitations discussion is honest (dependence of power gains on synthetic data quality) and the double-dipping robustness noted in Remark F.4 (the guardrail holds regardless of how the synthetic data were obtained) is a valuable and non-obvious property.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is moderate: GESPI is essentially a carefully designed wrapper that takes the min of a pooled-data procedure and a relaxed-level real-data guardrail. The intellectual leap is in recognizing the generality, not in a fundamentally new mechanism, and the proofs are relatively short. Reviewers valuing deep methodological novelty may find the contribution incremental.

The worst-case guarantee is α+ε, and the tighter α-level control depends on the TV distance d_{ℓ,Alg}(P,Q), which is generally not estimable from data. While the paper is upfront about this, it provides limited practical guidance on selecting ε (e.g., how to trade off the guaranteed level against expected power in a data-driven way), and the choice of ε is largely treated as a fixed hyperparameter in the experiments.

Baselines are somewhat thin in places. OnlyReal and OnlySynth are natural comparators, but the paper does not compare against alternative synthetic-data-leveraging approaches that could be applied to these specific tasks (e.g., SPI for the conformal case, or PPI-style estimators where assumptions permit), so it is hard to gauge how much of the gain is specific to GESPI versus generic to using synthetic data.

Some applications rely on somewhat bespoke synthetic-data constructions whose quality is not systematically varied. For example, in the protein experiment the synthetic errors are approximated by PAE-matrix means and low-confidence samples are filtered, and in the outlier-detection experiment the trimming proportion q is a tuning choice; the sensitivity of GESPI to these design decisions is only partially explored.

Minor presentational issues: notation is inconsistent across sections (e.g., D̂_N vs. D̃_N, Q̂ vs. Q̄), and some figures/tables in the appendix are hard to parse (e.g., the arrangement of Figure 7/9/10 panels). These do not undermine the claims but reduce readability.

strengths: Introduces a general and flexible framework (GESPI) that wraps any base statistical inference procedure and safely leverages synthetic data with distribution-free, finite-sample error control (α+ε) under no assumptions on the synthetic distribution.

Provides rigorous theoretical results: a risk upper bound in terms of total variation distance between loss distributions, a deterministic utility sandwich showing GESPI lies between the base and guardrail methods, and an impossibility result (Proposition E.1) justifying the ε admission cost.

Demonstrates broad applicability and empirical benefits across diverse tasks: conformal prediction, protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, outlier detection with FWER control, LLM win-rate comparison, mechanistic interpretability, and controlled simulations.

Experiments consistently show GESPI adapts to synthetic data quality: it attains error rates close to the nominal α with lower variance when synthetic data are high quality, while never exceeding α+ε in the worst case.
The paper is well-written, with clear explanations of the method, intuitions, and thorough experimental details that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic mechanism is conceptually simple—run the base method on pooled data and on real data at a relaxed level, then aggregate via min/max—which may be viewed as incremental relative to existing synthetic-powered inference and robust statistics ideas.

The general risk bound depends on an unobservable TV distance between loss distributions, offering limited practical guidance on when synthetic data will help; the only actionable guarantee is the conservative α+ε.

The method requires choosing ε and always sacrifices ε in worst-case error control. While ablations on ε are provided, there is no principled selection rule, and the computational overhead of running the base algorithm three times is not discussed.

In some experiments, the base method (OnlyReal) is trivial (e.g., 100% coverage with full prediction sets) due to extremely small real sample sizes, which makes the comparison less informative; the AlphaFold synthetic data construction relies on a heuristic PAE-based error proxy, though the method's validity does not depend on this.
The lower-bound tightness guarantees involve unquantified terms (τ, δ_n) that are not evaluated empirically, leaving the practical tightness of the two-sided guardrail version less clear.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely general framework (GESPI) that treats any risk-controlling inference procedure as a black box and wraps it to safely leverage synthetic data. This generality is a meaningful conceptual step beyond SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a), which is restricted to conformal prediction, and it enables applications to hypothesis testing, multiple testing, risk control, and predictive inference under one umbrella.

The theoretical results (Theorem 3.3, Theorem 3.4, Theorem F.2) are correctly stated and proven under mild, clearly articulated conditions (Condition F.1), and they provide finite-sample, distribution-free guarantees that hold even when the synthetic distribution is arbitrary. The formalization of the general inference problem in (4) and Table 1/S1 is clean and useful.

The paper is unusually broad in its empirical evaluation, covering image classification, AlphaFold protein structure prediction, out-of-distribution detection (single and multiple testing), LLM win-rate comparison, and mechanistic interpretability of a ViT. The AlphaFold and LLM-comparison applications are particularly interesting and non-trivial.

The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) is a nice addition: it formalizes why the α+ε relaxation is necessary, showing that uniform α-control over all synthetic distributions is unattainable in a nontrivial way.
Reproducibility is reasonable: the appendix provides detailed experimental setups, model choices, prompts, and per-class tables, which would allow others to reconstruct most experiments.
weaknesses: The novelty over SPI is incremental. The two central ingredients—(i) a guardrail run at α+ε and (ii) combining a synthetic-powered action with a real-data-only action—are inherited from or strongly parallel to Bashari et al. (2025a). The main addition is the black-box wrapper and the min/max aggregation in (5)/(6), which is conceptually simple; the 'always at least as good as base' property follows by construction (taking the max with Alg_α in (6)) rather than from a deep result.

The abstract overclaims. It states that GESPI 'adaptively defaults to the standard method using only real data when synthetic data are of low quality,' but the theory (and the paper's own Section 3.1) shows that when synthetic data are poor, GESPI falls back to the guardrail at α+ε, i.e., to a real-data-only method with strictly worse error control than the base method. This conflates 'utility never below base' with 'error control defaults to base' and misrepresents the safety guarantee.

The central theoretical bound, α + min{ε, c·d_{ℓ,Alg}(P,Q)}, is weak. The total-variation term d_{ℓ,Alg}(P,Q) is generally not small unless the synthetic and real distributions nearly coincide, so in practice the bound is essentially α+ε. The claimed 'adaptivity' (risk approaching α as synthetic quality improves) is not meaningfully captured by this bound; the sandwich in Theorem F.2 depends on τ and d̃, neither of which is estimable.

The empirical gains are modest and largely consist of variance reduction relative to the guardrail. In several reported cases (e.g., Admiral, Jay, White wolf in Table S3), GESPI attains exactly the guardrail bound, providing no benefit over simply running the base method at α+ε. The paper's headline claims of 'substantial gains' are not uniformly supported by the tables.

The variance-reduction argument (Figure S7/S8) aligns GESPI and OnlyReal at the same mean empirical coverage—a comparison the paper itself admits is 'not feasible in practice.' This makes the practical relevance of the variance-reduction claim unclear.

The AlphaFold experiment rests on a heuristic synthetic-data construction: true structures are unavailable, so per-residue error is approximated by the mean PAE row, and proteins with >50% proxy errors are discarded. The quality of this proxy is not validated, so the strong performance attributed to high-quality synthetic data is not well established.

The limitation discussion is thin. Section 5 mentions only that power gains depend on synthetic quality; it does not discuss the α+ε cost, the looseness of the TV bound, the assumption that synthetic data are i.i.d. from a single Q, or the difficulty of choosing ε.

strengths: Presents a general and elegant framework (GESPI) that wraps around any base statistical inference procedure via a simple aggregation (min/max, OR/AND, union/intersection), unifying conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided and multiple hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals under a single decision-theoretic formulation (Eq. 4, Tables 1 and S1).

Provides rigorous, distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees: worst-case error control at alpha+epsilon with adaptive tightening toward alpha as synthetic quality improves (Theorems 3.3 and F.2), plus a clean utility 'sandwich' guarantee showing the output is always at least as good as the base method and no worse than the guardrail (Theorem 3.4).

The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) is a thoughtful and important addition: it shows that uniformly controlling the loss at level alpha over all possible synthetic distributions forces one to effectively ignore the synthetic data, thereby justifying the epsilon relaxation rather than leaving it as an arbitrary design choice.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation across genuinely different domains (ImageNet conformal prediction, AlphaFold protein structure prediction, LLM win-rate comparison on AIME25/OlympiadBench, conformal outlier detection, and ViT mechanistic interpretability), consistently demonstrating near-nominal risk, reduced variance, and improved power, with graceful fallback when synthetic data are of low quality (e.g., Siberian Husky class).

Good reproducibility: the appendix specifies datasets, models (CLIP, AlphaFold2/ColabFold, DeepSeek/Qwen), synthetic-data generation procedures, score functions, and hyperparameters in substantial detail.
Honest treatment of limitations, including the explicit acknowledgment that power gains depend on synthetic data quality and that the epsilon budget is an 'admission cost' paid in the worst case.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea is a relatively direct generalization of SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a); the main conceptual novelty is the decision-theoretic abstraction and the three-way aggregation, which is elegant but not deeply surprising. The contribution is more a unification than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The epsilon 'admission cost' is a real, non-removable limitation: in the worst case the user's error rate is inflated to alpha+epsilon, which may be unacceptable in high-stakes settings. The paper offers limited principled guidance for selecting epsilon beyond empirical sensitivity plots (Figures S2, S4, S5).

The general bounds (Theorem 3.3, F.2) depend on total-variation distances between loss distributions that are generally uncomputable and can be loose, so the claim that the error rate 'decreases as synthetic quality improves' remains somewhat qualitative rather than practically quantifiable.

The advertised 'automatic adaptivity' is an emergent property of the guardrail structure rather than an explicit quality-detection or data-selection mechanism; it would help to clarify precisely when and why GESPI improves over the Guardrail baseline (the paper largely shows they are comparable in the high-quality regime).

Head-to-head comparison with the most closely related data-pooling methods is limited: SPI is only compared for conformal prediction (and relegated to the appendix), and PPI-style methods are not empirically benchmarked, while Synth+Real is included only as a non-guaranteed illustration.

Several experiments operate in extremely small-n regimes (n=10 proteins; n=15 questions) where the OnlyReal baseline is pathologically conservative (100% abstention in Figure 2a), which may exaggerate the perceived practical gains; a wider sweep over n and more realistic baselines would strengthen the empirical case.
Each individual application is evaluated relatively shallowly (single dataset/task per domain), so the breadth of the experiments partly comes at the cost of depth in any one setting.
